title: Goecha La and Dzongri trek: stage by stage from Yuksom
meta_description: Goecha La and Dzongri trek from Yuksom: stages, altitudes, huts vs tents, permits, guide rules, 2025–26 costs, best months and the View Point 1 limit.
summary: Goecha La is an 8–10 day return trek from Yuksom into Khangchendzonga National Park, climbing via Tshoka and Dzongri to View Point 1 at about 4,600 m. You need a park permit and a licensed guide; foreigners also need an agency. Go in April–May or October–November. Dzongri alone takes 4–5 days.

sections.heading: What the Goecha La trek actually is
paras: The Goecha La trail is the classic walk of West Sikkim. It starts at Yuksom, the village where Sikkim's first Chogyal was consecrated in 1642, and climbs north through Khangchendzonga National Park, set up in 1977 and inscribed in 2016 as India's first UNESCO mixed World Heritage Site. Over eight to ten days you go from cardamom fields and oak forest at 1,780 m to moraine and glacial lakes below the south face of Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on earth.

It is not a technical climb. There are no ropes, no fixed lines and, in a normal October or May, no snow crossings that need special gear. What makes it hard is altitude and length: several nights at or near 4,000 m, cold nights in tents, and long descents on stony trail that test knees more than lungs. Fit beginners do finish it, and the ones who do are those who walk slowly, drink water and accept a rest day at Dzongri. We think of it as the best mid-altitude trek in the eastern Himalaya for people with ten days and a modest budget.

sections.heading: Stage by stage from Yuksom
paras: The stages below follow the pattern most Yuksom agencies and organised groups use. Hours are walking time for an average group with breaks; altitudes are approximate and vary by a hundred metres or so between maps and GPS readings.

list: Yuksom to Sachen: a gentle start through warm, wet forest with several stream crossings on suspension bridges. Sachen is a camping clearing, not a village.
Sachen to Tshoka: a steady drop to the Prek Chu bridge, then a hard climb to Bakhim and on to Tshoka, the last settlement on the trail, where a few families run tea huts.
Tshoka to Dzongri: rhododendron and fir forest, wooden walkways near Phedang, then the open grass of Dzongri. Most people feel the altitude here first.
Dzongri Top: a 45–60 minute climb in the dark to about 4,200 m for sunrise across Kabru, Rathong, Kanchenjunga and Pandim.
Thansing to Lamuney: a short, flat day beside the moraine of the Onglathang valley, kept short on purpose so your body can adjust.
Lamuney to View Point 1: a 2–3 am start past Samiti Lake to reach the viewpoint as the first light hits Kanchenjunga and Pandim.

sections.heading: Dzongri only or the full Goecha La
paras: The Dzongri trek is the first half of the Goecha La route and back: Yuksom, Sachen or Tshoka, Dzongri, a dawn climb to Dzongri Top, then down again. It takes four to five days return and tops out at about 4,200 m. You get the single best mountain panorama of the whole route for half the days and half the cost, which is why we suggest it to families with fit teenagers, people on a short leave and anyone trying a Himalayan trek for the first time.

The full trek adds the Thansing valley, Samiti Lake and the dawn at View Point 1, where Pandim fills the sky in front of you and the Onglathang glacier sits below. It also adds three to five days, a second spell of nights near 4,000 m and a midnight start. If you have the days and you felt well at Dzongri, carry on. If Dzongri gave you a pounding headache, take the hint and walk down.

In winter, from December to February, some agencies still run Dzongri when snow allows, with frozen nights well below minus 10 °C. The upper valley beyond Thansing is often snowbound then, so the full Goecha La is mostly a spring and autumn trip.

sections.heading: Permits, guides and the View Point 1 rule
paras: These are the rules as we understand them for the 2025–26 seasons. They are set by the Sikkim Forest Department and the park authority, they have changed several times in recent years, and you should check current status before you travel.
list: Indian trekkers register at the Khangchendzonga National Park office and check post in Yuksom with photo ID and pay park entry and camping fees there.
A licensed local guide is mandatory for everyone. Solo trekking without a guide is not allowed, and permits are not issued without one.
Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, plus a trekking permit arranged through a registered Sikkim travel agency, normally for a group of two or more with a guide.
Permits and your waste may be checked again along the trail. Carry every wrapper back down; some seasons agencies log what goes up and what comes back.
View Point 1, at about 4,600 m, is where most groups are allowed to stop in recent seasons. The pass itself, at about 4,900 m, and View Point 2 have generally been closed to ordinary trekkers.
Weather, landslides on the Yuksom road and local decisions can close the trail at short notice, so keep one spare day in your plan.

sections.heading: Trekkers' huts, tents and where you sleep
paras: The Sikkim government runs simple trekkers' huts at Tshoka and Dzongri. Expect bare dormitory rooms with wooden floors or bunks, a shared toilet outside and nothing else: you bring your own sleeping bag and mat. They are cheap and warmer than a tent, but space is small and in peak weeks of October and May they fill with groups. Your guide or agency arranges them along with the permit; do not walk up assuming a bed.

Above Dzongri almost everyone camps. A good agency gives you two-person tents, a sleeping bag rated to about minus 10 °C, a foam mat, a dining tent and a toilet tent. If you hire a guide and cook yourself in Yuksom, check the sleeping bags with your own hands before you leave; cheap hired bags are the most common cause of a miserable night at Lamuney. Tshoka also has a couple of tea huts selling tea, noodles and biscuits in season.

sections.heading: What it costs in 2025–26
paras: There are two ways to do it. You can book an organised fixed-departure group with a national trekking company, or hire a guide, cook and porters through a small Yuksom agency for your own party. The figures below are indicative and per person unless stated.

list: A party of four or more brings the local-agency price down sharply, because guide and cook wages are shared.
Getting to Yuksom adds about ₹600–900 by shared jeep from Siliguri via Jorethang and Pelling, or ₹150–250 a seat from Pelling.
Ask whether the agency is registered with Sikkim Tourism, who the guide is, and what happens to your money if the trail closes.

sections.heading: When to go
paras: October and November give the clearest skies and the best odds of a cloud-free dawn at Dzongri Top and View Point 1, at the price of nights from minus 5 to minus 10 °C at Lamuney. April and May are warmer and bring rhododendrons in flower from Tshoka up to Phedang, but afternoons cloud over and views are hazier. December to February is snow season, workable for Dzongri with an experienced crew. June to September is the monsoon: leeches, landslides on the approach roads and trail closures. We do not suggest it.

sections.heading: Altitude sickness and staying well
list: Above about 3,000 m, raise your sleeping height slowly. The rest day at Dzongri is the most important day of the trek; do not trade it for speed.
Mild altitude sickness feels like a hangover: headache, nausea, no appetite, poor sleep. Do not go higher until it passes.
Confusion, stumbling, a wet cough or breathlessness at rest are emergencies. Descend at once, even at night, with your guide.
Talk to a doctor before the trip about acetazolamide (Diamox); it helps some people but is not a substitute for slow ascent.
Drink three to four litres a day, treat or boil stream water and skip alcohol above Tshoka.
Tell your guide honestly how you feel each morning. Rescue is on foot or by pony, and a helicopter is rare and weather-bound, so buy insurance that covers trekking to 5,000 m.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: Plan 8–10 days from Yuksom back to Yuksom, plus a day each way to reach Yuksom from NJP or Siliguri, which is 6–7 hours by road via Jorethang and Pelling. Add one spare day for weather or a closed road. Dzongri alone needs 4–5 days from Yuksom, so a Dzongri trip fits into a week from the plains.

faqs.q: Can I go all the way to the Goecha La pass?
faqs.a: In recent seasons most trekkers have been allowed only as far as View Point 1, at about 4,600 m. The pass itself, at about 4,900 m, and View Point 2 have generally been closed to ordinary groups. The view from View Point 1 is still the one most people come for. Rules are set by the forest department, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Goecha La suitable for first-time trekkers?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are fit and patient. The trail is not technical, but you spend several nights near 4,000 m and walk 5–10 hours on some days. Train for six weeks with stairs and long walks with a loaded pack. If you are unsure, start with the 4–5 day Dzongri trek, which gives the best panorama of the route at lower risk.

faqs.q: Can foreigners trek to Goecha La?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit and a trekking permit arranged through a registered Sikkim travel agency, usually for a group of two or more with a licensed guide. The agency handles the paperwork in Yuksom or Gangtok with your passport and photos. Permit conditions change from season to season, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Dzongri trek?
faqs.a: Yes. A licensed guide is mandatory for Dzongri as well as Goecha La, and the park office in Yuksom will not issue a permit to an unguided party. A local guide costs about ₹1,500–2,500 a day, which a group can share. Good guides also know where water is, when to turn back and how to book the trekkers' huts.

faqs.q: How cold does it get on the trek?
faqs.a: In October and November nights at Dzongri and Lamuney drop to about minus 5 to minus 10 °C, while days in the sun can feel like 10–15 °C. April and May are a few degrees milder. You need a down jacket, thermal layers, gloves, a warm hat and a sleeping bag rated to about minus 10 °C. Winter treks are colder still.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network on the Goecha La trail?
faqs.a: Do not count on it. You usually have a signal in Yuksom on Airtel, Jio or BSNL, but it fades soon after you leave the village and is patchy to absent beyond Tshoka. Tell family your expected return date before you start, download offline maps and carry a power bank, because there is no reliable charging above Yuksom.

faqs.q: What is the best month for Goecha La?
faqs.a: October and the first half of November give the clearest mountain views and stable weather, which is why they are the busiest weeks. April and May are best for rhododendrons in flower on the lower trail, with more afternoon cloud. Avoid June to September, when monsoon rain, leeches and landslides make the trek unpleasant and often impossible.

faqs.q: How much does the Goecha La trek cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively, ₹15,000–24,000 per person for a party of four to six hiring a guide, cook and porters through a Yuksom agency, or ₹20,000–30,000 per person with an organised national group. Add park fees, gear hire, insurance and about ₹600–900 for shared jeeps from Siliguri to Yuksom. Foreigners pay higher park fees.
